---
title: "orchestration & continuous training"
---

## coordinate the workflow

- orchestration coordinates tasks, dependencies, execution state, and failures across a workflow
- a task is one unit of work; a dependency states what must finish before another task can start
- a dag is a directed acyclic graph of those dependencies, useful for expressing steps without circular requirements
- a trigger starts a run, such as a schedule, new input data, or a code change

## tools and responsibilities

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| tool | definition | use case |
|---|---|---|
| nextflow | a workflow engine connecting processes and their inputs/outputs | coordinate bioinformatics tasks with containerised tools |
| prefect | a python workflow orchestration framework with tracked flows and tasks | coordinate python data and training steps with observable run state |
| airflow | a workflow scheduler that organises tasks into dags, with a web ui for monitoring and retrying runs | coordinate scheduled or event-triggered pipelines across heterogeneous systems and teams |
| aws step functions | a managed state-machine service that coordinates aws services and lambda functions from a json-based workflow definition | orchestrate a serverless pipeline that stays entirely within aws, such as ingest → validate → score |
| slurm | a cluster workload manager and scheduler | allocate resources to submitted tasks |
| subprocess | python’s interface for launching external commands | implement the small sequential runner below |

:::

- nextflow processes define task execution and data connections [process guide](https://docs.seqera.io/nextflow/process)
- in prefect, a flow coordinates work while tasks support tracked execution and configurable retries [flows](https://docs.prefect.io/v3/concepts/flows), [tasks](https://docs.prefect.io/v3/concepts/tasks)
- airflow's scheduler evaluates dags and launches due tasks; its ui is useful for seeing run history and failure points across many pipelines at once [airflow scheduler](https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/administration-and-deployment/scheduler.html)
- a step functions state machine is defined in amazon states language (asl), a json format describing states, transitions, and error handling; aws runs and tracks the execution for you [states language](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/concepts-amazon-states-language.html)
- slurm schedules compute; the workflow engine still decides task dependencies and downstream execution

## triggering a run from new data

- an event-driven trigger starts a workflow because something happened, rather than waiting on a fixed schedule — a file landing in object storage is a common trigger for a batch pipeline
- in aws, an s3 event notification fires when an object is created in a bucket (or a prefix within one); it can invoke a lambda function directly, or publish to sns/sqs/eventbridge for other services to pick up [s3 event notifications](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/EventNotifications.html)
- a common pattern: `s3 put → lambda → start a step functions execution` (or trigger an airflow dag run through its api); the lambda's job is to validate the event and kick off the real workflow, not to do the processing itself
- a lambda function is a small, stateless piece of code that runs in response to an event without you managing a server; use it for short glue logic like this trigger, not for long training or batch jobs [lambda overview](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/welcome.html)

```python
# illustrative lambda handler — reacts to an s3 put event and starts a step functions execution
import json
import boto3

sfn = boto3.client("stepfunctions")

def handler(event, context):
    record = event["Records"][0]["s3"]
    bucket = record["bucket"]["name"]
    key = record["object"]["key"]
    sfn.start_execution(
        stateMachineArn="arn:aws:states:us-east-1:123456789012:stateMachine:qc-pipeline",
        input=json.dumps({"bucket": bucket, "key": key}),
    )
```

- boto3 is the aws python sdk; use it to call aws services such as s3, lambda, step functions, and sagemaker from python code [boto3 documentation](https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/latest/index.html)
- keep the trigger idempotent: the same object landing twice, such as a retried upload, should not corrupt downstream state — check an output marker or the object's version id before reprocessing
- airflow and prefect both support starting a run from an external event through sensors or their api, rather than only from a schedule, if a dag-based orchestrator fits the rest of the system better than step functions [airflow scheduling](https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/administration-and-deployment/scheduler.html), [prefect deployments](https://docs.prefect.io/v3/concepts/deployments)

## start with a local runner

- the [automation exercise](../../examples/automation-demo.zip) includes `run_workflow.py`, which trains the synthetic model, validates its report, and writes a run manifest
- its central sequence is below; the complete script also handles run ids and failure records

```python
subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "lifecycle_demo.py", "--output", str(output)],
    check=True,
)
report = json.loads((output / "run.json").read_text())
score = check_candidate(report)
state.update(status="candidate", validation_auc=score)
```

- `check=True` raises an error when the command exits unsuccessfully, preventing normal progression to validation
- the example gate requires finite validation metrics, a score above the baseline, and validation roc auc of at least 0.75
- 0.75 is an illustrative threshold for this synthetic exercise; real criteria must reflect the task and consequences of errors
- `workflow-runs/<run-id>.json` records the current stage and outcome; a failed run is marked `failed`, while a passing run is only a `candidate`
- the runner refuses existing run ids to avoid overwriting prior results; it does not provide scheduling, distributed execution, or automatic resume

## retries and safe recovery

- a retry repeats a failed task; use bounded retries for transient problems such as a temporary connection failure
- backoff increases the delay between attempts so repeated failures do not overload a service
- a timeout limits how long a task can run; use it to stop stalled jobs
- do not automatically retry permanent schema errors or rejected candidates without changing the underlying cause
- keep writes idempotent, meaning repeated execution does not duplicate logical outputs, and record checkpoints only after successful output publication

## continuous training

- ct automates retraining when a trigger occurs; it still needs data checks and candidate validation before promotion [continuous training guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/mlops-continuous-delivery-and-automation-pipelines-in-machine-learning)
- separate “training completed” from “approved for release”; drift or new data can trigger investigation without forcing a replacement
- record input versions, workflow configuration, environment, metrics, and approval decisions with each candidate
- use orchestration when persistent state, retries, scheduling, or parallel dependencies justify more than a local script
